title: 部署 vLLM NVIDIA Dynamo 推理：生产环境指南
author: SitePoint Team
content:
Scaling large language model serving beyond naive HuggingFace generate() calls exposes a cascade of bottlenecks: contiguous memory allocation wastes GPU VRAM, serial request handling leaves expensive accelerators idle, and Python-level kernel dispatch overhead compounds with every forward pass. This guide walks through building a production inference service orchestrated with Docker Compose that unifies vLLM's PagedAttention scheduler with TorchDynamo-based CUDA graph replay.

How to Deploy vLLM with TorchDynamo CUDA Graph Inference

  1. Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and configure the Docker runtime for GPU passthrough.
  2. Verify GPU visibility inside containers with nvidia-smi and confirm driver/CUDA compatibility.
  3. Create the project directory structure with Docker Compose file, environment config, secrets, and model download script.
  4. Configure the Docker Compose stack with a model-downloader init container and the vLLM engine service with GPU reservations.
  5. Tune PagedAttention block size, swap space, and continuous batching parameters for your GPU and workload profile.
  6. Launch the stack, validate with the OpenAI-compatible API, and benchmark throughput using vLLM's serving benchmark tool.
  7. Harden the deployment with resource limits, Prometheus metrics, log rotation, and reverse-proxy authentication.

Table of Contents

  • Why vLLM + TorchDynamo Changes the Inference Equation
  • Architecture Overview of the vLLM TorchDynamo Inference Stack
  • Preparing the Host: NVIDIA Container Toolkit and Runtime Verification
  • Building the Docker Compose Deployment
  • Tuning PagedAttention and TorchDynamo Compilation for Throughput
  • Launching, Validating, and Benchmarking the Service
  • Production Hardening and Observability
  • Troubleshooting Common Deployment Failures
  • Next Steps

Why vLLM + TorchDynamo Changes the Inference Equation

Deploying vLLM with TorchDynamo-based CUDA graph replay in a production environment addresses these bottlenecks through two complementary mechanisms. vLLM's PagedAttention scheduler manages KV-cache memory in non-contiguous blocks, enabling continuous batching of concurrent requests without memory fragmentation. PyTorch's TorchDynamo compiler frontend (torch._dynamo) captures operation graphs at the dispatcher level, enabling CUDA graph replay that reduces kernel launch overhead across repeated inference calls. On short sequences, kernel launch overhead can account for 5-15% of decode-step time, making this a measurable win for autoregressive workloads.

Note: This guide covers TorchDynamo (PyTorch's compiler frontend, available since PyTorch 2.0) and CUDA graph replay as used within vLLM. NVIDIA Dynamo is a separate inference serving framework not covered here.

This guide walks through building a production inference service orchestrated with Docker Compose that unifies these technologies. Readers will configure GPU passthrough via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and construct a multi-service Docker Compose stack with annotated runtime flags. The guide also covers tuning PagedAttention block allocation, adjusting TorchDynamo compilation parameters, and validating throughput using vLLM's benchmarking tools.

Prerequisites: a Linux host with one or more NVIDIA GPUs, CUDA 12.x drivers installed, Docker Engine 24 or later, and Docker Compose CLI v2.20 or later (verify with docker compose version; legacy docker-compose v1 is not supported). Working familiarity with PyTorch and container networking is assumed.

Architecture Overview of the vLLM TorchDynamo Inference Stack

How vLLM's PagedAttention Manages GPU Memory

Traditional transformer serving frameworks allocate KV-cache memory in large contiguous blocks sized to the maximum possible sequence length. This approach wastes GPU VRAM on padding for shorter sequences and prevents memory reuse across requests. vLLM's PagedAttention replaces this with block-level KV-cache allocation, inspired by virtual memory paging in operating systems. vLLM divides the KV-cache into fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens per block) and allocates them on demand as it generates tokens. When a request completes, those blocks return to a free pool immediately available for new requests. This eliminates internal fragmentation and allows near-complete use of available GPU memory. At high concurrency, fragmentation in contiguous allocation schemes reduces effective throughput; without paged allocation, fragmentation can halve effective batch size above roughly 64 concurrent sequences (see Kwon et al., 2023 — "Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention" for quantitative analysis).

vLLM's PagedAttention replaces this with block-level KV-cache allocation, inspired by virtual memory paging in operating systems.

Where TorchDynamo Fits In

TorchDynamo operates at the PyTorch dispatcher level, intercepting Python bytecode to capture computation graphs before they reach the GPU. A backend, typically Inductor or TensorRT, compiles these captured graphs and replays them as CUDA graphs that bypass the standard Python-to-CUDA dispatch path. The result is reduced kernel launch overhead, particularly for the repeated decode steps in autoregressive generation where the same computational pattern executes thousands of times per request.

TorchDynamo is the compiler frontend within PyTorch (available since PyTorch 2.0), responsible for graph capture and compilation orchestration. In the context of vLLM serving, TorchDynamo graph capture and CUDA graph replay work alongside PagedAttention's memory scheduler rather than replacing it. vLLM manages its own compilation pipeline via CLI flags (--enforce-eager, --compilation-config in v0.6+), integrating with NVIDIA's CUDA toolchain for optimized graph execution on NVIDIA GPUs.

Deployment Topology

The annotated docker-compose.yml below implements this architecture. A topology diagram is not included in this guide. At the host level, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit exposes GPU devices to the Docker runtime. Docker Compose orchestrates two services: a model-downloader init container that pulls and caches model weights to a named volume, and the vLLM engine container that loads the model with PagedAttention scheduling and CUDA graph replay enabled. GPU allocation flows through the deploy.resources.reservations.devices block in the Compose specification, mapping physical GPUs to the vLLM engine container. The Compose file configures a healthcheck directly on the vLLM engine service. The full Docker Compose file implementing this topology appears in the next section.

Preparing the Host: NVIDIA Container Toolkit and Runtime Verification

Installing and Configuring the NVIDIA Container Toolkit

The NVIDIA Container Toolkit enables Docker containers to access host GPU devices. Installation on Ubuntu/Debian follows the apt-based workflow:

# Add the NVIDIA Container Toolkit repository
curl -fsSL https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/gpgkey | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg
curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/libnvidia-container/stable/deb/nvidia-container-toolkit.list | \
  sed 's#deb https://#deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/nvidia-container-toolkit-keyring.gpg] https://#g' | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-container-toolkit.list

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-container-toolkit

# Configure the Docker runtime to use the NVIDIA runtime
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker

# Restart Docker to apply changes
sudo systemctl restart docker

# Verify the runtime entry exists in daemon.json
cat /etc/docker/daemon.json
# Expected output should include: "default-runtime": "nvidia" or a "runtimes" block with "nvidia"

Verifying GPU Visibility and Driver Compatibility

After toolkit installation, verify that containers can see host GPUs:

docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.4.1-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi

The output should display the driver version (e.g., 550.x), CUDA version (12.4), and available GPU memory for each device. Common failure modes include mismatched driver and toolkit versions (the toolkit requires a minimum driver version matching its CUDA support), omitting the --gpus flag entirely, and cgroup v2 configuration issues on newer Ubuntu installations where the NVIDIA runtime may need explicit cgroup driver settings.

CUDA and PyTorch Version Matrix

Pinning specific versions prevents silent incompatibilities, particularly with TorchDynamo backend stability:

Mixing CUDA 12.4 host drivers with containers built against CUDA 12.1 generally works due to CUDA's forward compatibility, but TorchDynamo's Inductor backend generates PTX code targeting a specific compute capability, and mismatches can trigger silent fallbacks to eager mode.

Building the Docker Compose Deployment

Project Directory Structure

vllm-dynamo-deploy/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── .env
├── .gitignore
├── secrets/
│   └── hf_token.txt
├── configs/
│   └── vllm_args.yaml
└── scripts/
    └── download_model.py

The Complete Docker Compose File

# docker-compose.yml — Production vLLM + TorchDynamo CUDA Graph Inference Stack
# Requires Docker Compose CLI v2.20+ (verify with: docker compose version)

volumes:
  model-cache:
    driver: local

secrets:
  hf_token:
    file: ./secrets/hf_token.txt

services:
  # Init container: downloads and caches model weights to a named volume
  # NOTE: Access to Llama-2 models requires license acceptance at
  # https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf
  # Ensure your HF account is approved before proceeding.
  model-downloader:
    image: python:3.11-slim
    volumes:
      - model-cache:/models
      - ./scripts/download_model.py:/download_model.py:ro
    environment:
      - MODEL_NAME=${MODEL_NAME:-meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf}
    secrets:
      - hf_token
    command: >
      bash -c "pip install --timeout 60 -q 'huggingface_hub==0.24.0' && python /download_model.py"
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 4g
          cpus: "2"
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure
        max_attempts: 3

  # Primary inference engine
  vllm-engine:
    image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.6.2
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    volumes:
      - model-cache:/models:ro
    environment:
      # Must be OFF in production — blocking serializes CUDA calls
      - CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0
      # Enable verbose logging during initial compilation (set to 0 in steady state)
      - TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE=${TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE:-0}

      # --- Hugging Face ---
      - HF_HUB_CACHE=/models
      - HF_HOME=/models
      - MODEL_NAME=${MODEL_NAME:-meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf}

      # vLLM controls compilation via CLI flags (--enforce-eager, --compilation-config).
      # Standard TorchDynamo env vars (TORCHDYNAMO_BACKEND, TORCH_COMPILE_BACKEND)
      # are not vLLM control surfaces and should not be set here.
    secrets:
      - hf_token
    # HF_TOKEN is read from /run/secrets/hf_token at runtime — not from environment
    command: >
      --model /models/${MODEL_NAME_SHORT:-Llama-2-7b-chat-hf}
      --tensor-parallel-size ${TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE:-1}
      --gpu-memory-utilization ${GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION:-0.90}
      --max-model-len ${MAX_MODEL_LEN:-4096}
      --block-size ${BLOCK_SIZE:-16}
      --swap-space ${SWAP_SPACE:-4}
      --max-num-seqs ${MAX_NUM_SEQS:-256}
      --max-num-batched-tokens ${MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS:-8192}
      --dtype ${DTYPE:-auto}
      # CUDA graphs are enabled by default. Add --enforce-eager to disable them.
    ipc: host
    ulimits:
      memlock: -1
      stack: 67108864
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options:
        max-size: "100m"
        max-file: "5"
    deploy:
      resources:
        reservations:
          devices:
            - driver: nvidia
              count: ${GPU_COUNT:-1}
              capabilities: [gpu]
        limits:
          cpus: "${CPU_LIMIT:-8}"
          memory: ${MEMORY_LIMIT:-32g}
    restart: unless-stopped
    depends_on:
      model-downloader:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    healthcheck:
      test:
        - "CMD-SHELL"
        - "python -c \"import urllib.request, sys; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health') and sys.exit(0)\""
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 120s

Key annotations: CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 must remain off in production as enabling it serializes all CUDA operations, destroying throughput. The --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 flag allocates 90% of available GPU memory (after model weights are loaded) to the KV-cache pool. The remaining 10% covers CUDA context overhead, activation buffers, and fragmentation headroom. Model weights are loaded before this allocation runs. vLLM enables CUDA graph replay for decode steps by default; to disable it (e.g., for debugging), add --enforce-eager to the command block. The ipc: host setting is required for NCCL shared-memory communication when using TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE > 1, and is safe to leave enabled for single-GPU deployments as well.

Important: The depends_on condition service_completed_successfully requires Docker Compose CLI v2. The version: "3.8" key has been removed from this file because it is deprecated in Compose v2 CLI and its presence may cause confusion with Compose v3 schema expectations. Verify your Compose CLI version with docker compose version and confirm the condition is honored with docker compose config.

Security: The HF token is injected via Docker secrets (mounted at /run/secrets/hf_token) rather than environment variables. This prevents exposure through docker inspect. Create the secret file before first run: mkdir -p secrets && echo "hf_your_actual_token" > secrets/hf_token.txt. Add secrets/ to .gitignore.

Model Download Script

The download logic is extracted into a separate Python script to avoid shell injection risks from inline YAML command blocks:

# scripts/download_model.py
import os
import sys
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def main():
    model_name = os.environ.get("MODEL_NAME")
    if not model_name or "/" not in model_name:
        logger.error("MODEL_NAME must be set and in 'org/repo' format. Got: %r", model_name)
        sys.exit(1)

    # Read token from Docker secret mount — never from env var
    token = None
    secret_path = "/run/secrets/hf_token"
    if os.path.exists(secret_path):
        with open(secret_path) as f:
            token = f.read().strip()
    if not token:
        logger.warning("HF token not found at %s; proceeding unauthenticated (gated models will fail)", secret_path)

    repo_name = model_name.split("/")[-1]
    local_dir = f"/models/{repo_name}"
    logger.info("Downloading %s to %s", model_name, local_dir)

    try:
        from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
        snapshot_download(
            repo_id=model_name,
            local_dir=local_dir,
            token=token,
            local_files_only=False,
        )
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.error("Download failed: %s", exc, exc_info=True)
        sys.exit(1)

    logger.info("Download complete: %s", local_dir)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Environment Variables and .env Configuration

# .env — Environment variable reference
# SECURITY: NEVER commit this file. Add .env to .gitignore.
# HF_TOKEN must NOT appear here. Use Docker secrets:
#   mkdir -p secrets && echo "hf_your_actual_token" > secrets/hf_token.txt
#   Add secrets/ to .gitignore
MODEL_NAME=meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf
MODEL_NAME_SHORT=Llama-2-7b-chat-hf
TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE=1
GPU_COUNT=1
GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION=0.90
DTYPE=auto
MAX_NUM_SEQS=256
MAX_MODEL_LEN=4096
BLOCK_SIZE=16
SWAP_SPACE=4
MAX_NUM_BATCHED_TOKENS=8192
TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE=0
CPU_LIMIT="8"
MEMORY_LIMIT=32g

Each variable maps directly to a vLLM CLI argument or runtime environment setting. DTYPE=auto allows vLLM to select the optimal precision based on the model configuration and GPU architecture (bfloat16 on Ampere/Ada/Hopper; float16 on Volta; check model config for overrides). MAX_NUM_SEQS caps the maximum number of sequences processed concurrently in the continuous batching scheduler. MODEL_NAME_SHORT must exactly match the subdirectory name created by snapshot_download (which uses the repo name after the /, e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat-hf).

Multi-GPU Tensor Parallelism Setup

For multi-GPU deployments, set TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE to match the number of GPUs, and set the deploy block's count field to the same value (e.g., TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE=2 and GPU_COUNT=2 for two GPUs, or 4 for four GPUs). To target specific devices, set the NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable (e.g., NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1) in the vllm-engine service. The ipc: host setting in the Compose file is required when TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE > 1 because NCCL requires shared memory for intra-node communication, and Docker's default IPC namespace isolation will cause NCCL errors without this setting. The Compose file above includes ipc: host unconditionally, which is safe for single-GPU deployments as well.

A word on interconnect: tensor parallelism communication overhead depends heavily on GPU interconnect topology. NVLink 3.0 (A100 SXM) provides 600 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth; NVLink 4.0 (H100 SXM) provides 900 GB/s. PCIe 4.0 x16 provides 32 GB/s bidirectional, making cross-GPU tensor parallelism heavily bandwidth-constrained. On PCIe-only systems, tensor parallelism across more than 2 GPUs can introduce communication bottlenecks that negate the benefit of additional GPUs, particularly for smaller models where the compute-to-communication ratio is low.

Tuning PagedAttention and TorchDynamo Compilation for Throughput

PagedAttention Block Size and Swap Space

The --block-size parameter controls the number of tokens per KV-cache block. A block size of 16 produces finer-grained allocation with less internal waste per block but increases bookkeeping overhead. A block size of 32 reduces management overhead at the cost of potentially wasting more memory per block for short sequences. For workloads dominated by long sequences (2048+ tokens), block size 32 tends to perform better per vLLM's documentation. For chatbot-style workloads with highly variable sequence lengths, block size 16 tends to yield higher effective memory use due to reduced per-block waste.

The --swap-space parameter (in GiB) enables overflow of KV-cache blocks to CPU memory when GPU memory is exhausted. This prevents request rejection but introduces PCIe transfer latency. Set it to 4-8 GiB as a safety buffer rather than relying on it for steady-state operation.

# Launch vLLM with tuned PagedAttention flags and monitor GPU memory
docker compose up -d vllm-engine

# Monitor real-time GPU memory and utilization
nvidia-smi dmon -s um -d 5
# Use `nvidia-smi dmon --help` to confirm column labels for your driver version

TorchDynamo Graph Capture and CUDA Graphs

Inside the container, TorchDynamo captures computation graphs during the first N inference requests (the warm-up phase). Subsequent requests replay precompiled CUDA graphs, eliminating per-request compilation overhead. The number of warm-up requests depends on input shape variety; vLLM's CUDA graph capture uses fixed shape buckets, so warm-up completes once all encountered shapes have been compiled.

For custom entrypoints requiring fine-grained control over TorchDynamo behavior, the configuration must be applied before any vLLM or model initialization occurs:

# custom_entrypoint.py — TorchDynamo configuration overrides
# Must be imported/executed BEFORE any vLLM or model initialization.
import sys
import logging
import torch

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

TORCH_MAJOR, TORCH_MINOR = (int(x) for x in torch.__version__.split(".")[:2])

try:
    import torch._dynamo as dynamo

    # Increase graph variant cache (default: 8). Higher = more memory.
    dynamo.config.cache_size_limit = 16

    # Never suppress errors in production — silent eager fallback hides regressions.
    dynamo.config.suppress_errors = False

    # Dynamic shape support: API changed across versions.
    if (TORCH_MAJOR, TORCH_MINOR) < (2, 2):
        # PyTorch < 2.2: legacy attribute
        dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = True
    else:
        # PyTorch >= 2.2: use torch.compile dynamic flag at call site instead.
        # torch.compile(..., dynamic=True) — configure in vLLM CLI via --compilation-config
        logger.info(
            "PyTorch %s: automatic_dynamic_shapes removed; use --compilation-config or "
            "torch.compile(dynamic=True) at call site.",
            torch.__version__,
        )

except AttributeError as exc:
    logger.error("TorchDynamo config error (check PyTorch version %s): %s", torch.__version__, exc)
    sys.exit(1)

Setting suppress_errors = True in production is dangerous because it silently falls back to eager execution without CUDA graph replay, degrading throughput without any visible error. The suppress_errors = False setting shown above is the correct production configuration.

Important: All dynamo.config assignments must occur before any import that loads model weights or triggers compilation. If placed after vLLM engine initialization, the settings are silently ignored. The automatic_dynamic_shapes attribute was removed in PyTorch 2.2; the version guard above prevents AttributeError on newer PyTorch releases.

Continuous Batching Parameters

The interplay between --max-num-seqs and --max-num-batched-tokens controls how the continuous batching scheduler batches requests. Increasing --max-num-seqs raises aggregate throughput by packing more requests into each batch iteration but increases per-request latency due to larger batch sizes.

These are starting points. Optimal values depend on model size, average sequence length, and whether the workload is prefill-heavy (long prompts) or decode-heavy (long completions).

Launching, Validating, and Benchmarking the Service

Starting the Stack

# Create the secrets directory and token file before first run
mkdir -p secrets
echo "hf_your_actual_token" > secrets/hf_token.txt

docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f vllm-engine
# Watch for:
#   "Loading model weights..."
#   Compilation-related log lines during warm-up
#   "Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000" — indicates readiness

The model-downloader init container runs first, pulling weights into the named volume. The vllm-engine container starts only after the downloader completes successfully. Initial startup, including model loading and first compilation pass, typically takes 60-180 seconds for a 7B-parameter model on a single A100. Larger models or slower GPUs will take proportionally longer.

Sending Test Requests via the OpenAI-Compatible API

Before sending requests, confirm the served model name by querying the models endpoint:

# Verify the exact model name vLLM is serving
curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/models | python -m json.tool
# The "id" field in the response is the model name to use in subsequent requests
curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Llama-2-7b-chat-hf",
    "prompt": "Explain the concept of PagedAttention in three sentences.",
    "max_tokens": 128,
    "temperature": 0.7
  }' | python -m json.tool

# In the response, examine the "usage" block:
# "prompt_tokens": N — tokenized input length
# "completion_tokens": M — generated output length
# "total_tokens": N+M

Note: The model field in the request must match the value reported by GET /v1/models. If there is a mismatch, vLLM returns a 404 error.

Throughput Benchmarking with vLLM's Built-in Tool

# Clone the vLLM repository at the matching version for benchmark scripts
git clone --branch v0.6.2 https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git
cd vllm

# Download the ShareGPT dataset required by the benchmark
wget --timeout=60 --tries=3 \
  https://huggingface.co/datasets/anon8231489123/ShareGPT_Vicuna_unfiltered/resolve/main/ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json

# Verify file is non-empty before proceeding
[ -s ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json ] || { echo "Download failed or empty"; exit 1; }

# Run serving benchmark with request rate sweeps
# NOTE: The --dataset-name flag may be named --dataset in some vLLM versions.
# Run: python benchmarks/benchmark_serving.py --help | grep dataset
# to confirm the correct flag name for your version.
python benchmarks/benchmark_serving.py \
  --backend openai \
  --base-url http://localhost:8000 \
  --model Llama-2-7b-chat-hf \
  --dataset-name sharegpt \
  --dataset-path ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json \
  --num-prompts 500 \
  --request-rate 10

# Key metrics in the output:
# - Throughput (tokens/sec): aggregate generation speed
# - TTFT (time-to-first-token): latency before first token arrives
# - ITL (inter-token latency): average time between successive tokens
# - GPU utilization %: via nvidia-smi during the benchmark run

Sweeping --request-rate from 1 to the point where TTFT degrades reveals the concurrency ceiling for the deployment. A well-tuned vLLM stack with CUDA graph replay on an A100 typically achieves 1.3-2x higher throughput than eager-mode execution at equivalent latency targets, per vLLM's published benchmarks.

Production Hardening and Observability

Resource Limits, Restart Policies, and Logging

The deploy.resources.limits block in the Compose file caps CPU and memory to prevent a single container from starving host resources. The restart: unless-stopped policy ensures automatic recovery from transient failures. Docker restarts OOM-killed containers (exit code 137), which can trigger a crash loop if the model is too large for available memory. Monitor for repeated 137 exits and adjust memory limits or --gpu-memory-utilization accordingly. The Compose file configures json-file logging with max-size and max-file options to prevent log accumulation from consuming disk space. For centralized log aggregation, replace the logging driver with a structured driver targeting systems like Loki or Elasticsearch.

Security note: Port 8000 is exposed with no built-in authentication. The OpenAI-compatible API endpoint has no auth mechanism. For any non-localhost exposure, place a reverse proxy (e.g., nginx, Caddy) in front of the service with API key enforcement or use network-level access controls.

Prometheus Metrics and Grafana Dashboards

vLLM exposes a /metrics endpoint in Prometheus format, providing real-time visibility into requests in flight, KV-cache block utilization, batch sizes, and per-request latency histograms. A standard Prometheus scrape configuration targeting localhost:8000/metrics captures these metrics. Check the vLLM GitHub repository's examples directory for community-maintained Grafana dashboard configurations; availability may vary by version.

Model Hot-Swapping and Rolling Updates

Because model weights reside on a named Docker volume, swapping models requires only updating the weight files on the volume and restarting the engine container:

docker compose up -d --no-deps vllm-engine

The --no-deps flag prevents restarting the model-downloader service. This restarts the engine container immediately; in-flight requests will be dropped. True zero-downtime model swapping requires an external load balancer (e.g., nginx, HAProxy, or a Kubernetes ingress) with health-check-gated traffic shifting to a parallel instance. Only after the new instance passes health checks (GET /health returns 200) should traffic be routed to it.

Troubleshooting Common Deployment Failures

"CUDA out of memory" During Model Load

Reduce --gpu-memory-utilization from 0.90 to 0.85 (or 0.80 if other GPU consumers are present), lower --max-model-len, or verify that no competing GPU processes (other containers, desktop environments) are consuming VRAM via nvidia-smi. This error surfaces when the utilization flag is set too high, leaving insufficient VRAM for activation buffers and CUDA context overhead after model weights and KV-cache are allocated.

TorchDynamo Compilation Errors or Fallbacks

Set TORCHDYNAMO_VERBOSE=1 in the environment to surface where graphs break and why compilation fails in container logs. Graph breaks occur when TorchDynamo encounters Python operations it cannot trace (data-dependent control flow, unsupported operators). Each graph break prevents CUDA graph replay for that subgraph. The suppress_errors=True configuration should be used only during development diagnostics and never in production, as it masks performance regressions.

Container Exits with Code 137 (OOM-Killed)

The Linux OOM killer sends this signal when KV-cache swap to CPU memory (controlled by --swap-space) consumes more host RAM than the Docker memory limit permits. Increase the memory limit in the deploy.resources.limits block, or reduce --swap-space to constrain CPU memory usage.

Next Steps

The annotated docker-compose.yml is a reusable starting point for any vLLM deployment. Natural extensions include enabling speculative decoding for further latency reduction, serving multiple LoRA adapters from a single base model instance, and migrating the Compose stack to Kubernetes using the NVIDIA GPU Operator for cluster-scale orchestration.
aiSummary: 一份生产级部署指南，介绍如何在 Docker Compose 中运行带 TorchDynamo CUDA 图推理的 vLLM，涵盖 GPU 直通、内存调优和多 GPU 张量并行。
oneSentenceSummary: 一份生产级部署指南，介绍如何在 Docker Compose 中运行带 TorchDynamo CUDA 图推理的 vLLM，涵盖 GPU 直通、内存调优和多 GPU 张量并行。
summary: 本指南针对大语言模型服务中的瓶颈问题——连续 VRAM 分配、串行请求处理以及 Python 层面的内核调度开销——通过在 Docker Compose 栈中部署带 TorchDynamo 的 CUDA 图重放的 vLLM 来加以解决。文章解释了 vLLM 的 PagedAttention 调度器如何借鉴操作系统虚拟内存思想，将连续的 KV-cache 分配替换为块级分页；并说明 TorchDynamo 如何在 PyTorch 分发器层面捕获计算图，从而实现 CUDA 图重放以减少内核启动开销。文章提供了一份完整的带注释的 docker-compose.yml，包含模型下载器的初始化容器、GPU 预留、通过 Docker secrets 注入 Hugging Face token 以及生产加固标志。文中还包含 CUDA/PyTorch/vLLM 版本兼容性矩阵、PagedAttention 块大小和交换空间的参数调优指导，以及需要 NCCL 共享内存支持的多 GPU 张量并行设置。文章澄清其覆盖的是 PyTorch 的 TorchDynamo，而非独立的 NVIDIA Dynamo 推理框架。 notable gaps：文章在讨论多 GPU 的部分中途截断，且承诺的可观测性、基准测试和故障排除章节尚未完成。

mainPoints.point: vLLM 的 PagedAttention 消除 KV-cache 内存碎片
mainPoints.explanation: 与传统框架按最大序列长度分配连续内存块（因填充浪费 VRAM）不同，vLLM 将 KV-cache 划分为固定大小的块（默认 16 个 token）并按需分配。这使得 GPU 内存利用率接近满配，并防止在高并发下有效批量大小退化——连续方案在并发序列超过约 64 时，碎片化可能导致批量大小减半。

mainPoints.point: TorchDynamo CUDA 图重放降低解码步骤的内核启动开销
mainPoints.explanation: TorchDynamo 在 PyTorch 分发器层面拦截 Python 字节码，捕获计算图，并以 CUDA 图形式重放，从而绕过 Python 到 CUDA 的分发路径。在短序列场景下，内核启动开销占解码步骤耗时的 5-15%，因此这对自回归工作负载带来可测量的吞吐量提升。

mainPoints.point: 生产部署需要严格的版本锁定与密钥管理
mainPoints.explanation: 将 CUDA 主机驱动与容器构建混用可能触发静默的 TorchDynamo 回退到 eager 模式。指南提供了版本矩阵（CUDA 12.1+ 搭配匹配的 PyTorch/vLLM 版本对）。Hugging Face token 必须使用挂载在 /run/secrets 的 Docker secrets，而非环境变量，以避免通过 docker inspect 泄露。

mainPoints.point: 多 GPU 张量并行需要 ipc:host 以支持 NCCL 共享内存通信
mainPoints.explanation: 当 TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE > 1 时，Docker 默认的 IPC 命名空间隔离会导致 NCCL 错误。设置 ipc: host 是实现节点内 GPU 通信的必要条件。GPU 分配通过 deploy.resources.reservations.devices 控制，count 需与 TENSOR_PARALLEL_SIZE 匹配。

mainPoints.point: 生产环境中必须禁用 CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING
mainPoints.explanation: 启用 CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING 会使所有 CUDA 操作串行化，从而彻底破坏吞吐量，该标志仅应用于调试。--gpu-memory-utilization 参数设为 0.90 表示在加载模型权重后，将剩余 GPU 内存的 90% 分配给 KV-cache 池，留出 10% 给 CUDA 上下文开销和碎片缓冲空间。

生产环境中 CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 必须保持关闭——启用它会串行化所有 CUDA 操作，破坏吞吐量。
